headline: GaussianGPT Brings Autoregressive Thinking to 3D Scene Generation
lede: Most 3D generative models today lean on diffusion or flow-matching — holistic refinement processes borrowed from image synthesis. A team at the Technical University of Munich is proposing a different lineage: treat a three-dimensional scene the way GPT treats a sentence, building it one discrete token at a time. The result, GaussianGPT, can generate, complete, and outpaint 3D scenes within a single pipeline.
body:
The underlying representation is **3D Gaussian splatting**, a technique that encodes a scene as a cloud of tiny, oriented ellipsoids — each carrying position, opacity, and colour — rather than a mesh or voxel grid. Gaussians are cheap to render and increasingly common as a neural-rendering substrate, but generating them from scratch has proved difficult. Diffusion models, the current default, refine a noisy scene globally until it converges, giving limited control over which parts of a scene are synthesised first.

GaussianGPT reframes the problem as sequence modelling. A *sparse 3D convolutional autoencoder* with *vector quantisation* first compresses Gaussian primitives into a grid of discrete tokens — essentially a codebook of scene patches. A causal transformer then predicts those tokens one by one, using *3D rotary positional embeddings* to keep spatial relationships coherent across the sequence. The approach is directly analogous to how a language model predicts the next word, but the "vocabulary" here is quantised chunks of 3D geometry and appearance.

The payoff is flexibility that diffusion models struggle to offer. Because the model maintains an explicit distribution over the scene at every generation step, it can be stopped mid-sequence to complete a partial scene, or conditioned on an existing region to outpaint beyond its boundaries — capabilities that require bespoke re-training or inversion tricks in diffusion pipelines. Temperature sampling, a standard language-model knob, gives direct control over how diverse or conservative the output geometry is.

The authors situate autoregressive modelling as a *complementary* paradigm rather than a wholesale replacement for diffusion. The compositional inductive bias of next-token prediction — the assumption that a scene can be built up part by part — may be better suited to structured, bounded environments like rooms than to the globally correlated statistics of natural images, where diffusion remains formidable. Whether the approach scales to complex outdoor scenes or fine-grained object detail is the open question the paper leaves on the table.

GaussianGPT is joint work by Nicolas von Lützow, Barbara Rössle, Katharina Schmid, and Matthias Nießner at TU Munich's Visual Computing group. Code is listed as forthcoming on GitHub; the paper is available on arXiv as 2603.26661.

concepts.definition: A scene representation that models a 3D environment as a collection of tiny, semi-transparent ellipsoids (Gaussians), each defined by position, orientation, scale, colour, and opacity. Because Gaussians can be rendered very quickly via rasterisation, they have become a popular alternative to neural radiance fields (NeRF) for novel-view synthesis and now generative modelling.

A modelling strategy in which outputs are produced one unit at a time, each conditioned on everything generated so far. GPT-style language models are the canonical example: they predict the next token given all previous tokens. GaussianGPT applies the same idea to 3D scene tokens rather than words.

A compression technique that maps continuous high-dimensional vectors to the nearest entry in a finite codebook of learned 'prototype' vectors. In GaussianGPT it turns continuous Gaussian parameters into discrete indices, making next-token prediction tractable. The same idea underpins VQ-VAE and the tokenisers used in image generation models like DALL-E.

A method for encoding position information into transformer attention that encodes relative distances rather than absolute positions, by rotating query and key vectors in the complex plane. In GaussianGPT the technique is extended to three spatial dimensions so the transformer can reason about where in 3D space each token sits.

A generative modelling framework, closely related to diffusion, that learns a vector field mapping noise to data via smooth continuous flows. It has become a strong competitor to standard diffusion models for image and 3D generation. GaussianGPT's autoregressive approach contrasts with both diffusion and flow-matching paradigms.

repos.summary: The official code release for GaussianGPT, hosted by lead author Nicolas von Lützow. At the time of publication the repository was listed as coming soon. It is expected to contain the sparse 3D convolutional autoencoder, vector-quantised tokeniser, and the causal transformer used for autoregressive scene generation.
